analysis.one_liner: Locks in Gulf red snapper catch quotas and shields Gulf fishermen from bycatch reduction requirements.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Commerce Committee without a vote; it would have fixed a 9,120,000-pound annual red snapper catch quota and barred any rule that cut harvests to reduce shrimp-trawl bycatch.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written Gulf red snapper catch quotas into federal law through 2001 — 9.12 million pounds a year, split 51% for commercial boats and 49% for recreational anglers — overriding any conflicting regulation. It would have guaranteed recreational anglers a 4-fish daily bag limit and a 15-inch minimum size, and barred the Commerce Department from closing the fishery on any date the Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Council had not recommended. It also would have shielded the catch from any requirement tied to bycatch reduction devices and ordered a fast review of whether shrimp-trawl turtle excluder devices could count as bycatch reduction devices.
analysis.who_benefits: Gulf of Mexico commercial red snapper fishermen would get a statutory quota — about 4.65 million pounds a year — locked in regardless of future stock assessments. Charter boats and recreational anglers would get the 49% share, a guaranteed 4-fish daily bag limit, and protection from early season closures. Shrimp trawlers would benefit if turtle excluder devices were certified as bycatch reduction devices, sparing them from installing or upgrading separate gear, and the whole harvest would be exempt from any device-performance condition that reduced the quota.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gulf commercial, charter, and shrimp fleets

how_it_helps.text: Sets a fixed aggregate red snapper quota of 9.12 million pounds a year for 1998 through 2001, split 51% commercial and 49% recreational, and states it prevails "notwithstanding any other provision of law," so federal managers could not lower it.

Guarantees recreational anglers a 4-fish daily bag limit and a 15-inch minimum size through 2001, and bars the Secretary of Commerce from setting any red snapper closure date inconsistent with a recommendation of the Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Council.

Provides that the harvest cannot be subjected to any condition on bycatch reduction device performance that would reduce the catch, and requires the National Marine Fisheries Service to finish a review by the end of 1998 and, if warranted, certify turtle excluder devices as functioning bycatch reduction devices — a step that could spare shrimp trawlers from additional gear requirements.
Orders a peer-reviewed study of how much bycatch reduction the devices actually achieve in the Gulf, with a report to Congress — giving the industry and managers data on the devices' performance.

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on the red snapper stock itself — a public resource still recovering from overfishing. Shrimp trawls are a leading source of juvenile red snapper mortality, and the bill would remove the main tool (bycatch reduction requirements) managers had to address that while quotas stayed fixed through 2001. Federal fishery managers would lose the power to close the fishery or condition the catch on device performance, and future commercial fishermen and seafood consumers would bear the consequences if the stock's recovery slipped.
analysis.who_pays_short: The recovering red snapper fish stock

drawbacks.text: By writing fixed quotas into law "notwithstanding any other provision of law" and barring closures that depart from Gulf Council recommendations, the bill would strip federal fishery managers of the ability to cut the catch or close the fishery if the stock worsened during 1998–2001.

Freeing the harvest from bycatch device conditions and fast-tracking turtle excluder devices as certified bycatch reduction devices would leave shrimp-trawl bycatch of juvenile red snapper largely unaddressed — and juvenile bycatch is the main obstacle to rebuilding the stock — while the bill's own study of how well the devices work would not even begin until May 2001, after the rules were already set.

Locking quotas and size limits in statute through 2001 prevents annual adjustment to new stock assessments, an honest supporter would acknowledge, in a fishery whose numbers were actively disputed between scientists and industry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bought Gulf fleets and anglers three years of regulatory certainty, but it did so by statute instead of by science: quotas, bag limits, and size limits were fixed in law before the bill's own bycatch study could inform them, and managers lost the emergency brake of closing the fishery. For an overfished stock whose biggest problem was shrimp-trawl bycatch of young snapper, short-term harvest certainty came at the real risk of a slower recovery — a cost that would land later, on the same fishermen and on the public that owns the resource.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read it twice and sent it to the Commerce Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Sessions of Alabama introduced the bill on July 31, 1998, and spoke about it when he introduced it.
Two Republican senators signed on as cosponsors.

The bill was referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the day it was introduced; the action history shows no further committee or floor action of any kind for the rest of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, existing federal management of the red snapper fishery — including bycatch reduction requirements and the authority to close the fishery — stayed in place, so the default winners were the stock's recovery and the managers, anglers, and future fishermen who depend on it. The shrimp and snapper fleets that the bill was written for gained nothing beyond the status quo.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill

sides.party_line_note: Only three senators are on record — Sessions and two Republican cosponsors — and the bill never reached a floor vote, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: Shrimp trawls are the leading source of juvenile red snapper killed as unwanted bycatch, and the bill would exempt the snapper harvest from bycatch-device conditions and expedite certifying shrimp trawls' turtle excluder devices as bycatch reduction devices — sparing the fleet from adding or upgrading gear. The fleet's savings would come at the cost of slower recovery of a publicly owned fish stock.

The bill writes a 51% share of a fixed 9.12-million-pound annual quota into federal law, immune from stock-based adjustments or device conditions through 2001. That is harvest certainty for the fleet, but it locks in taking from a stock that was still rebuilding.

industries.industry: Charter and for-hire recreational fishing fleet
industries.note: The bill guarantees the recreational share, a 4-fish daily bag limit, and protection from early season closures that the fleet's customers dislike — though crew members would be barred from keeping snapper while a vessel is for hire. In the short run this aligns with ordinary anglers; over the long run it depends on a stock the bill's own bycatch rules would do little to rebuild.

The bill overrides the fisheries service's existing red snapper regulations, blocks device-performance conditions that would cut the catch, and bars closures inconsistent with the regional council's recommendations — removing the tools managers use to respond to stock data.
